title: Why Great Whites Aren’t Purely Cold‑Blooded
description: Great white sharks keep part of their body temperature above the surrounding water, a trait that lets them hunt in chilly seas. This partial warm‑bloodedness fuels their status as apex predators.
narration: GREAT WHITE SHARK IS NOT WHAT YOU THINK You assume every shark is a cold‑blooded fish, its body temperature matching the surrounding sea. In reality, the great white is partially warm‑blooded, using specialized blood vessels to keep its core warmer than the water and sustain high‑speed bursts during hunts, giving it the stamina to chase fast prey like seals even in the cold currents off California and South Africa. Scientists have identified a rete mirabile—a counter‑current heat exchanger—in great whites that conserves metabolic heat. This partial endothermy, also seen in mako and salmon sharks, enables the species to remain active in waters as cool as 10 °C, supporting its hunting of marine mammals in temperate zones. The physiological boost lets them patrol deeper, colder layers while maintaining muscle efficiency, a factor that distinguishes them from fully ectothermic sharks. That heat edge powers its reputation as the ocean’s top predator, allowing it to out‑swim rivals and dominate the coastal food chain.
